A short list, curated. Everything here is free unless marked, and everything here is genuinely worth the hours.

The official documentation

Resource What it is When
The Rust Programming Language "The Book" — the canonical introduction Days 1–20
Rust by Example runnable snippets, no prose When you need a syntax reminder
The Rustonomicon unsafe, FFI, the real memory model Only when you write unsafe
The Rust Reference normative language spec When two sources disagree
std API docs the standard library Daily
The Cargo Book build system reference Module 03.01
Rust API Guidelines how to design a public crate Before publishing
The Rust Performance Book Nicholas Nethercote's optimisation guide Module 03.05
Rust Design Patterns idioms and anti-patterns After the Book
Comprehensive Rust Google's 4-day course A fast structured review

Books

Book Author Read it when
Programming Rust (2nd ed) Blandy, Orendorff, Tindall You want depth and precision, with C++ comparisons
Rust for Rustaceans Jon Gjengset After the Book — traits, async internals, API design
Rust Atomics and Locks Mara Bos Concurrency, memory ordering, building your own primitives — free online
Zero to Production in Rust Luca Palmieri Building a production web service, end to end
Command-Line Rust Ken Youens-Clark Learning by writing eight real CLI tools
The Rust Programming Language (book form) Klabnik, Nichols The Book, on paper

Rust Atomics and Locks is free at https://marabos.nl/atomics/. Rust for Rustaceans is the single best "next step" book.

Video

Channel / series Why
Crust of Rust (Jon Gjengset) Long, live-coded deep dives: lifetimes, Send/Sync, channels, Arc. The best Rust video content that exists
Let's Get Rusty Short, structured, beginner-friendly
Jon Gjengset's streams Building real things slowly, with mistakes
RustConf talks (YouTube) The "Rust in production" track is consistently good
fasterthanlime Extremely detailed debugging and internals write-ups

Reading, weekly

Source Content
This Week in Rust The newsletter. Crates, RFCs, jobs, talks — read the top section
r/rust Discussion, release announcements
users.rust-lang.org The forum where hard questions get good answers
Rust Blog Release notes — read them, they explain new features
Inside Rust Language team working notes

Finding crates

Site Use
crates.io the registry
docs.rs rendered docs for every crate and version — your default reference
lib.rs curated, categorised, better discovery than crates.io
blessed.rs opinionated "use this one" recommendations per domain
Are we web yet? web ecosystem status
Are we game yet? gamedev ecosystem status
Are we embedded yet? embedded status

blessed.rs is the fastest way to stop wondering which of five HTTP clients to pick.

Tools to install

bacon deserves a mention: it watches your project and shows errors in a pane while you type. It changes how the edit-compile loop feels.

Communities

Where Culture
Rust Discord fast help, #beginners is welcoming
users.rust-lang.org slower, higher-quality answers
r/rust news and discussion
Rust Zulip language development, for contributors
Local meetups search "Rust" + your city; most are beginner-friendly

How to ask a good question: post the code, the full error, and what you tried. Better: post a minimal reproducible example — building it usually solves the problem before you post.

Conferences and talks

  • RustConf (US, annual) — talks on YouTube
  • Rust Nation UK (London)
  • EuroRust (rotating European city)
  • Rust India and regional meetups
  • Rust Belt Rust, RustFest (historically)

The production-experience talks are the most useful: what broke, what they measured, what they would do differently.

Learning by reading code

The fastest way to write idiomatic Rust is to read good Rust. In rough order of accessibility:

Project Why read it
ripgrep clean CLI + high-performance internals
fd small, readable, excellent clap usage
bat terminal output done well
serde the derive-macro architecture
axum extractors and tower integration
tokio the executor and runtime internals (hard)
polars large-scale data engineering in Rust
hyperfine small, well-tested CLI
alacritty a real application, not a library
rust-analyzer a huge codebase doing real compiler work

Start with fd — it is small enough to read in an afternoon and idiomatic throughout.

Anti-resources

Honest list of things that waste time:

  • Tutorials that predate 2021. Editions changed use paths, closures and IntoIterator; pre-2018 tutorials will actively mislead you.
  • Copy-pasting from Stack Overflow answers older than the crate version you use. Check the date and the crate version in the answer.
  • Trying to learn unsafe, Pin and macros in week one. They are advanced for a reason.
  • Rewriting a C library "to learn Rust". Pick something you actually want to exist.
  • Benchmarking without --release. You will conclude Rust is slow.

The one-paragraph summary

Read The Book once, type everything. Then read Rust for Rustaceans. Then build something real, and read docs.rs for every crate you touch. Ask in users.rust-lang.org when you are stuck for more than 30 minutes. Read fd's source. That path, in that order, is the fastest one that actually works.
